'''John Bannister Goodenough''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɡ|ʊ|d|ɪ|n|ʌ|f}} {{respell|GUUD|in|uf}}; July 25, 1922 – June 25, 2023) was an American materials scientist, a [[solid-state physicist]], and a [[Nobel laureate in chemistry]]. From 1986 he was a professor of Materials Science, Electrical Engineering and Mechanical Engineering,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.me.utexas.edu/ |title=Welcome to the Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering|website=Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering}}</ref>  at the [[University of Texas at Austin]]. He is credited with
identifying the [[Goodenough–Kanamori rules]] of the sign of the magnetic [[superexchange]] in materials, with developing materials for computer [[Random Access Memory|random-access magnetic memory]] and with inventing cathode materials for [[lithium-ion batteries]].

Goodenough was awarded the [[National Medal of Science]], the [[Copley Medal]], the [[Enrico Fermi Award|Fermi Award]], the [[Charles Stark Draper Prize|Draper Prize]], and the [[Japan Prize]]. The [[John B. Goodenough Award]] in materials science is named for him. In 2019, he was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] alongside [[M. Stanley Whittingham]] and [[Akira Yoshino]]; at 97 years old, he became the oldest Nobel laureate in history.<ref name="NYT-20191009" /> From August 27, 2021, until his death, he was the oldest living Nobel Prize laureate.

==Personal life and education==
John Goodenough was born in [[Jena]], Germany, on July 25, 1922,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11512001.html |title=John B. Goodenough |work=[[American Institute of Physics]]}}</ref> to American parents, [[Erwin Ramsdell Goodenough]] (1893–1965) and Helen Miriam (Lewis) Goodenough.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TOYkAAAAYAAJ&q=%22Helen+Miriam+Lewis%22 |title=Myth for Moderns: Erwin Ramsdell Goodenough and Religious Studies in America, 1938–1955 |publisher=Scarecrow Press |year=1997 |first=Eleanor Bustin |last=Mattes |isbn=978-0-8108-3339-5 |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> He came from an academic family. His father, a graduate student at [[University of Oxford|Oxford]] when John was born, eventually became a professor of religious history at [[Yale]].<ref name="NobelPrize.org" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Collection: Erwin Ramsdell Goodenough papers {{!}} Archives at Yale |url=https://archives.yale.edu/repositories/12/resources/3926 |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=archives.yale.edu}}</ref> His brother [[Ward Goodenough|Ward]] became an anthropology professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ward H. Goodenough papers |url=https://www.penn.museum/collections/archives/findingaid/552845 |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology}}</ref> John also had two half-siblings from his father's second marriage: [[Ursula Goodenough]], emeritus professor of [[biology]] at [[Washington University in St. Louis]]; and Daniel Goodenough, emeritus professor of [[biology]] at [[Harvard Medical School]].<ref name="McFadden-2023" />

In his school years Goodenough suffered from [[dyslexia]]. At the time, dyslexia was poorly understood by the medical community, and Goodenough's condition went undiagnosed and untreated.<ref name="McFadden-2023" /> Although his primary schools considered him "a backward student," he taught himself to write so that he could take the entrance exam for [[Groton School]], the boarding school where his older brother was studying at the time.<ref name="McFadden-2023" /><ref name="Gregg-2016">{{Cite web |last=Gregg |first=Helen |date=Summer 2016 |title=His Current Quest |url=https://mag.uchicago.edu/science-medicine/his-current-quest# |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=The University of Chicago Magazine |language=en}}</ref> He was awarded a full scholarship.<ref name="NobelPrize.org">{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/goodenough/biographical/ |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US}}</ref> At Groton, his grades improved and he eventually graduated at the top of his class in 1940.<ref name="McFadden-2023" /><ref>{{cite news |last1=LeVine |first1=Steve |date=February 5, 2015 |title=The man who brought us the lithium-ion battery at the age of 57 has an idea for a new one at 92 |url=http://qz.com/338767/the-man-who-brought-us-the-lithium-ion-battery-at-57-has-an-idea-for-a-new-one-at-92/ |access-date=February 5, 2015 |work=[[Quartz (publication)]] |publisher=[[Atlantic Media Company]]}}</ref> He also developed an interest in exploring nature, plants, and animals.<ref>The Powerhouse: America, China, and the Great Battery War. 2016. S. Levine.</ref> Although he was raised an atheist, he converted to [[Protestantism|Protestant Christianity]] in high school.<ref name="Gregg-2016" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Friedman |first=Gail |date=Fall 2019 |title=Battery Genius |url=https://groton.myschoolapp.com/ftpimages/542/download/download_4149703.pdf |journal=Groton School Quarterly |pages=19–21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |agency=Eternity News |date=October 14, 2019 |title=Winners of this year's Nobel prizes follow Jesus |url=https://www.eternitynews.com.au/world/winners-of-this-years-nobel-prizes-follow-jesus/,%20https://www.eternitynews.com.au/world/winners-of-this-years-nobel-prizes-follow-jesus/ |access-date=May 8, 2021 |website=www.eternitynews.com.au |language=en-AU}}</ref>

After Groton, Goodenough graduated ''summa cum laude'' from [[Yale College|Yale]], where he was a member of [[Skull and Bones]].<ref name="Goodenough-2008">{{cite book |last=Goodenough |first=John B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ufMTLWx30q0C |title=Witness to Grace |publisher=[[PublishAmerica]] |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-4626-0757-0 |via=[[Google Books]]}}</ref> He completed his coursework in early 1943 (after just two and a half years) and received his degree in 1944,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Belli |first=Brita |date=October 9, 2019 |title=Nobel laureate John Goodenough '44 inspires next generation of scientists |url=https://news.yale.edu/2019/10/09/nobel-laureate-john-goodenough-44-inspires-next-generation-scientists |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=YaleNews |language=en}}</ref> covering his expenses by tutoring and grading exams.<ref name="Goodenough-2008" /> He had initially sought to enlist in the military following the [[Attack on Pearl Harbor|Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor]], but his mathematics professor convinced him to stay at Yale for another year so that he could finish his coursework, which qualified him to join the [[United States Army Air Corps|U.S. Army Air Corps']] meteorology department.<ref name="Gregg-2016" /><ref name="Goodenough-2008" />

After World War II ended, Goodenough obtained a master's degree and a Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of Chicago]], the latter in 1952.<ref name="Gregg-2016" /><ref name="thesis-goodenough-1952">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302038451 |title=A theory of the deviation from close packing in hexagonal metal crystals |date=1952 |publisher=[[The University of Chicago]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Goodenough |first=John B. |id={{ProQuest|302038451}}|url-access=subscription |oclc=44609164}}</ref> His doctoral supervisor was [[Clarence Zener]], a theorist in [[electrical breakdown]]; he also worked and studied with physicists, including [[Enrico Fermi]] and [[John Alexander Simpson|John A. Simpson]]. While at Chicago, he met Canadian history graduate student Irene Wiseman.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2019/goodenough/biographical/ | title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2019 }}</ref><ref name="ucalum">{{Cite news |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/john-b-goodenough-shares-nobel-prize-invention-lithium-ion-battery |title=University of Chicago alum John B. Goodenough shares Nobel Prize for invention of lithium-ion battery |last=Olinto |first=Angela |date=September 9, 2019 |work=UChicago News |access-date=October 9, 2019 |language=en}}</ref> They married in 1951.<ref name="McFadden-2023" /><ref name="NobelPrize.org" /> The couple had no children.<ref name="McFadden-2023" /> Irene died in 2016.<ref name="ucalum" />

Goodenough [[centenarian|turned 100]] on July 25, 2022.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Manthiram |first1=Arumugam |author1-link=Arumugam Manthiram |title=John Goodenough's 100th Birthday Celebration: His Impact on Science and Humanity |journal=[[ACS Energy Letters]] |date=July 8, 2022 |volume=7 |issue=7 |pages=2404–2406 |doi=10.1021/acsenergylett.2c01343 |bibcode=2022ACSEL...7.2404M |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsenergylett.2c01343 |access-date=November 3, 2022 |language=en |issn=2380-8195|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He died at an assisted living facility in [[Austin, Texas]], on June 25, 2023, one month shy of what would have been his 101st birthday.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/news/goodenough-nobel-laureate-who-gave-the-world-li-ion-batteries-passes-away/article67010369.ece|title=Goodenough, Nobel laureate who gave the world Li-ion batteries, passes away|date=June 26, 2023|website=www.thehindubusinessline.com|accessdate=June 26, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.utexas.edu/2023/06/26/ut-mourns-lithium-ion-battery-inventor-and-nobel-prize-recipient-john-goodenough/|title=UT Mourns Lithium-Ion Battery Inventor and Nobel Prize Recipient John Goodenough|publisher=UTexas.edu|accessdate=June 26, 2023|date=June 26, 2023}}</ref><ref name="McFadden-2023">{{cite news |last1=McFadden |first1=Robert |title=John B. Goodenough, 100, Dies; Nobel-Winning Creator of the Lithium-Ion Battery |work=The New York Times |date=June 26, 2023 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/06/26/science/john-goodenough-dead.html |access-date=June 26, 2023}}</ref>

==Career and research==
[[File:John Goodenough - National Medal of Science, 2011.webm|thumb|Goodenough discusses his research and career.]]Over his career, Goodenough authored more than 550 articles, 85 book chapters and reviews, and five books, including two seminal works, ''Magnetism and the Chemical Bond'' (1963)<ref>{{cite web |last=Jacoby |first=Mitch |date=September 13, 2017 |title=Goodenough wins 2017 Welch Award |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/95/i37/Goodenough-wins-2017-Welch-Award.html |access-date=October 10, 2019 |work=[[Chemical and Engineering News]]}}</ref> and ''Les oxydes des metaux de transition'' (1973).<ref name="chemworld 2014" />

===MIT Lincoln Laboratory===
After his studies, Goodenough was a research scientist and team leader at the [[MIT Lincoln Laboratory]] for 24 years. At MIT, he was part of an interdisciplinary team responsible for developing [[Random Access Memory|random-access magnetic memory]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ryan |first=Dorothy |date=October 9, 2019 |title=Longtime MIT Lincoln Laboratory researcher wins Nobel Prize in Chemistry |url=https://www.ll.mit.edu/news/longtime-mit-lincoln-laboratory-researcher-wins-nobel-prize-chemistry |access-date=February 23, 2024 |website=MIT Lincoln Laboratory}}</ref> His research focused on [[magnetism]] and on the [[metal–insulator transition]] behavior in [[transition-metal oxides]]. His research efforts on RAM led him to develop the concepts of cooperative orbital ordering, also known as a cooperative [[Jahn–Teller distortion]], in [[oxide]] materials.<ref name="RSC1">{{cite web |title=Royal Society of Chemistry – John B Goodenough Award |url=http://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/JohnBGoodenoughAward/ |access-date=January 20, 2015 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> They subsequently led him to develop (with [[:ja:金森順次郎|Junjiro Kanamori]]) the [[Goodenough–Kanamori rules]], a set of semi-empirical rules to predict the sign of the magnetic [[superexchange]] in materials; superexchange is a core property for [[high-temperature superconductivity]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=J. B. Goodenough |author-link=John B. Goodenough |year=1955 |title=Theory of the Role of Covalence in the Perovskite-Type Manganites [La, M(II)]MnO<sub>3</sub> |url=http://doklady.belnauka.by/jour/article/view/403 |journal=Physical Review |volume=100 |issue=2 |page=564 |bibcode=1955PhRv..100..564G |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.100.564}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=John B. Goodenough |author-link=John B. Goodenough |year=1958 |title=An interpretation of the magnetic properties of the perovskite-type mixed crystals La<sub>1−x</sub>Sr<sub>x</sub>CoO<sub>3−λ</sub> |journal=Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids |volume=6 |issue=2–3 |page=287 |doi=10.1016/0022-3697(58)90107-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=J. Kanamori |year=1959 |title=Superexchange interaction and symmetry properties of electron orbitals |journal=Journal of Physics and Chemistry of Solids |volume=10 |issue=2–3 |page=87 |bibcode=1959JPCS...10...87K |doi=10.1016/0022-3697(59)90061-7}}</ref>

===University of Oxford===
[[File:Inorganic-chemistry-lab-Oxford-plaque.jpg|thumb|[[Blue plaque]] erected by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] commemorating work towards the rechargeable lithium-ion battery at Oxford]]
The U.S. government eventually terminated Goodenough's research funding, so during the late 1970s and early 1980s, he left the United States and continued his career as head of the [[Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory]] at the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name="RSC1" /> Among the highlights of his work at Oxford, Goodenough is credited with significant research essential to the development of commercial [[Li-ion battery|lithium-ion rechargeable batteries]].<ref name=RSC1/> Goodenough was able to expand upon previous work from [[M. Stanley Whittingham]] on battery materials, and found in 1980 that by using Li<sub>x</sub>CoO<sub>2</sub> as a lightweight, high energy density [[cathode]] material, he could double the capacity of lithium-ion batteries.

Although Goodenough saw a commercial potential of batteries with his LiCoO<sub>2</sub> and LiNiO<sub>2</sub> cathodes and approached the [[University of Oxford]] with a request to patent this invention, it refused. Unable to afford the patenting expenses with his academic salary, Goodenough turned to UK's [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] in [[Harwell, Oxfordshire|Harwell]], which accepted his offer, but under the terms, which provided zero [[Royalty payment|royalty]] payment to the inventors John B. Goodenough and [[Koichi Mizushima (scientist)|Koichi Mizushima]]. In 1990, the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment|AERE]] licensed Goodenough's patents to [[Sony Corporation]], which was followed by other battery manufacturers. It was estimated, that the AERE made over 10 million [[British pounds]] from this licensing.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}}

The work at [[Sony]] on further improvements to Goodenough's invention was led by [[Akira Yoshino]], who had developed a scaled up design of the battery and manufacturing process.<ref name="CNN Nobel">{{cite web | url = https://www.cnn.com/2019/10/09/us/john-goodenough-nobel-prize-trnd/index.html | title = John B. Goodenough just became the oldest person, at 97, to win a Nobel Prize |first=  Allen  | last = Kim | date = October 9, 2019 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | publisher =[[CNN]] }}</ref> Goodenough received the [[Japan Prize]] in 2001 for his discoveries of the materials critical to the development of lightweight high energy density rechargeable lithium batteries,<ref>{{cite web|title=The 2001 (17th) Japan Prize|url=https://www.japanprize.jp/en/prize_past_2001_prize01.html |website= Japan Prize Foundation|access-date=October 10, 2019|language=en}}</ref> and he, Whittingham, and Yoshino shared the 2019 [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] for their research in lithium-ion batteries.<ref name="CNN Nobel"/>

===University of Texas===
From 1986, Goodenough was a professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] in the [[Cockrell School of Engineering]] departments of Mechanical Engineering and [[Electrical Engineering]].<ref>{{cite news|title=UT professor, 81, is mired in patent lawsuit |first=Jim |last=Henderson |date=June 5, 2004 |work=Houston Chronicle |url=http://www.chron.com/default/article/UT-professor-81-is-mired-in-patent-lawsuit-1662323.php |access-date=August 26, 2011}}</ref> During his tenure there, he continued his research on ionic conducting solids and electrochemical devices; he continued to study improved materials for batteries, aiming to promote the development of [[electric vehicles]] and to help reduce human dependency on [[fossil fuels]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/the-battery-pioneer-who-at-age-96-keeps-going-and-going-1533807001 | title = The Battery Pioneer Who, at Age 96, Keeps Going and Going | first=  Sarah | last= MacFarlene | date = August 9, 2018 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | work = [[The Wall Street Journal]] }}</ref> [[Arumugam Manthiram]] and Goodenough discovered the polyanion class of cathodes.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Masquelier |first1=Christian |last2=Croguennec |first2=Laurence|author2-link=Laurence Croguennec |title=Polyanionic (Phosphates, Silicates, Sulfates) Frameworks as Electrode Materials for Rechargeable Li (or Na) Batteries |doi=10.1021/cr3001862 |journal=Chemical Reviews |volume=113 |issue=8 |pages=6552–6591 |year=2013|pmid=23742145 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Manthiram | first1 = A. | last2 = Goodenough | first2 = J. B. | doi = 10.1016/0378-7753(89)80153-3 | title = Lithium insertion into Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> frameworks | journal = Journal of Power Sources | volume = 26 | issue = 3–4 | pages = 403–408 | year = 1989 | bibcode = 1989JPS....26..403M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Manthiram | first1 = A. | last2 = Goodenough | first2 = J. B. | doi = 10.1016/0022-4596(87)90242-8 | title = Lithium insertion into Fe<sub>2</sub>(MO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> frameworks: Comparison of M = W with M = Mo | journal = Journal of Solid State Chemistry | volume = 71 | issue = 2 | pages = 349–360 | year = 1987 | bibcode = 1987JSSCh..71..349M | doi-access = free }}</ref> They showed that positive electrodes containing [[polyanion]]s, e.g., [[sulfate]]s, produce higher voltages than oxides due to the [[inductive effect]] of the polyanion. The polyanion class includes materials such as lithium-iron [[phosphates]] that are used for smaller devices like power tools.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://news.uchicago.edu/story/john-b-goodenough-shares-nobel-prize-invention-lithium-ion-battery | title = University of Chicago alum John B. Goodenough shares Nobel Prize for invention of lithium-ion battery | first=  Louise | last = Lerner | date = October 9, 2019 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | publisher = [[The University of Chicago]] }}</ref> His group also identified various promising [[electrode]] and [[electrolyte]] materials for solid oxide fuel cells.<ref name="chemworld 2014">{{cite web | url = https://www.chemistryworld.com/features/goodenough-rules/8099.article | title=  Goodenough rules | first = Bea | last= Perks |date = December 22, 2014 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | work = [[Chemistry World]] }}</ref> He held the Virginia H. Cockrell Centennial Chair in Engineering.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.me.utexas.edu/faculty/faculty-directory/goodenoughn|title=John Goodenough – Department of Mechanical Engineering|publisher=University of Texas|access-date=October 10, 2019}}{{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Goodenough still worked at the university at age 98 as of 2021,<ref>[https://news.utexas.edu/2019/10/09/nobel-prize-in-chemistry-goes-to-john-goodenough-of-the-university-of-texas-at-austin/ Nobel Prize in Chemistry Goes to John Goodenough of The University of Texas at Austin] (October 9, 2019)</ref> hoping to find another breakthrough in battery technology.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://qz.com/338767/the-man-who-brought-us-the-lithium-ion-battery-at-57-has-an-idea-for-a-new-one-at-92/ |title=The man who brought us the lithium-ion battery at the age of 57 has an idea for a new one at 92|last=LeVine|first=Steve|date=February 5, 2015|publisher=Quartz|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160305003001/http://qz.com/338767/the-man-who-brought-us-the-lithium-ion-battery-at-57-has-an-idea-for-a-new-one-at-92/ |archive-date=March 5, 2016}}</ref><ref name=cse2017-2/>

On February 28, 2017, Goodenough and his team at the University of Texas published a paper in the [[Scientific journal|journal]] ''[[Energy and Environmental Science]]'' on their demonstration of a [[glass battery]], a low-cost all-solid-state battery that is noncombustible and has a long [[Charge cycle|cycle life]] with a high volumetric [[energy density]], and fast rates of charge and discharge. Instead of liquid electrolytes, the battery uses glass electrolytes that enable the use of an [[alkali]]-metal [[anode]] without the formation of [[dendrites]].<ref name=C6EE02888H>{{cite journal |title=Alternative strategy for a safe rechargeable battery |first1=M.H. |last1=Braga |first2=N.S. |last2=Grundish |first3=A.J. |last3=Murchison |first4=J.B. |last4=Goodenough |journal=[[Energy and Environmental Science]] |volume=10 |pages=331–336 |date=December 9, 2016 |doi=10.1039/C6EE02888H|doi-access=}}</ref><ref name=cse2017-2>{{cite web|url= https://news.utexas.edu/2017/02/28/goodenough-introduces-new-battery-technology |title=Lithium-Ion Battery Inventor Introduces New Technology for Fast-Charging, Noncombustible Batteries|date=February 28, 2017|publisher=[[Cockrell School of Engineering]] |access-date=March 11, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2017-02/uota-lbi022817.php |title=Lithium-ion battery inventor introduces new technology for fast-charging, noncombustible batteries|date=February 28, 2017|publisher=EurekAlert!}}</ref> However, this paper was met with widespread skepticism by the battery research community and remains controversial after several follow-up works. The work was criticized for a lack of comprehensive data,<ref name="Lacey-2017">{{Cite web|last=Lacey|first=Matt|date=March 29, 2017|title=On the skepticism surrounding the "Goodenough battery"|url=http://lacey.se/2017/03/29/on-the-skepticism-surrounding-the-goodenough-battery/|access-date=November 13, 2020|website=Matt Lacey|language=en-us}}</ref> spurious interpretations of the data obtained,<ref name="Lacey-2017" /> and that the proposed mechanism of battery operation would violate the [[first law of thermodynamics]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Steingart|first1=Daniel A.|last2=Viswanathan|first2=Venkatasubramanian|date=January 17, 2018|title=Comment on "Alternative strategy for a safe rechargeable battery" by M. H. Braga, N. S. Grundish, A. J. Murchison and J. B. Goodenough, Energy Environ. Sci., 2017, 10, 331–336|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/2018/ee/c7ee01318c|journal=Energy & Environmental Science|language=en|volume=11|issue=1|pages=221–222|doi=10.1039/C7EE01318C|bibcode=2018EnEnS..11..221S |issn=1754-5706|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In April 2020, a patent was filed for the glass battery on behalf of Portugal's [[Laboratório Nacional de Energia e Geologia|National Laboratory of Energy and Geology]] (LNEG), the [[University of Porto]], Portugal, and the University of Texas.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thedriven.io/2020/04/06/li-ion-co-inventor-patents-glass-battery-that-could-upturn-auto-industry/|title=Li-ion co-inventor patents glass battery that could upturn auto industry|last=Schmidt|first=Bridie|date=April 6, 2020|website=The Driven|language=en-US|access-date=April 7, 2020}}</ref>

===Advisory work===
In 2010, Goodenough joined the technical advisory board of Enevate, a [[Lithium–silicon battery|silicon-dominant Li-ion battery]] technology startup based in [[Irvine, California]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ocbj.com/news/2019/oct/09/irvine-based-enevate-adviser-goodenough-shares-nob/|title=Enevate Adviser Shares Nobel|date=October 9, 2019|website=OCBJ|language=en-US|access-date=February 28, 2020}}</ref> Goodenough also served as an adviser to the [[Argonne National Laboratory#User facilities and centers|Joint Center for Energy Storage Research (JCESR)]], a collaboration led by [[Argonne National Laboratory]] and funded by the [[United States Department of Energy|Department of Energy]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mag.uchicago.edu/science-medicine/his-current-quest|title=His current quest|website=The University of Chicago Magazine|language=en|access-date=January 28, 2020}}</ref> From 2016, Goodenough also worked as an adviser for Battery500, a national consortium led by [[Pacific Northwest National Laboratory|Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL)]] and partially funded by the [[U.S. Department of Energy]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.utexas.edu/2016/07/27/doe-funds-battery-research-consortium/|title=Battery Research Consortium Chosen by DOE to Advance Electric Cars|date=July 27, 2016|website=UT News|language=en-US|access-date=January 28, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.energy.gov/science/articles/charging-development-lithium-ion-batteries|title=Charging Up the Development of Lithium-Ion Batteries|website=Energy.gov|language=en|access-date=January 28, 2020}}</ref>

==Distinctions and awards==
[[File:John B. Goodenough (2010).jpg|thumb|right|Goodenough receiving the 2009 [[Enrico Fermi Award]] from U.S. Energy Secretary [[Steven Chu]].]]
Goodenough was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 1976 for his work designing materials for electronic components and clarifying the relationships between the properties, structures, and chemistry of substances. He was also a member of the American [[National Academy of Sciences]] and its [[French Academy of Sciences|French]], [[Spanish Royal Academy of Sciences|Spanish]], and [[National Academy of Sciences, India|Indian]] counterparts.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.nae.edu/105796/John-B-Goodenough | title = John B. Goodenough | date = 2014 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | work = [[National Academy of Engineering]]}}</ref> In 2010, he was elected a [[Foreign Member of the Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite web |title=John Goodenough |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/john-goodenough-11514/ |access-date=March 20, 2012 |publisher=Royal Society}}</ref> The [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] grants a [[John B. Goodenough Award]] in his honor.<ref name="RSC1" /> [[The Electrochemical Society]] awards a biannual [[John B. Goodenough Award of The Electrochemical Society]].<ref>{{cite news |title=ECS Creates Biannual John B. Goodenough Award |url=https://www.electrochem.org/press/john-b-goodenough-award/ |access-date=November 17, 2024 |work=ECS |date=July 25, 2022}}</ref>

Goodenough received the following awards:
* [[Enrico Fermi Award|Fermi Award]] (2009), alongside metallurgist [[Siegfried S. Hecker|Siegfried Hecker]]<ref>{{cite press release | url = https://www.aps.org/publications/capitolhillquarterly/201004/fermiaward.cfm | title = Secretary Chu Names 2009 Enrico Fermi Award Winners | publisher = [[APS Physics]] | date = April 2010 | access-date = October 10, 2019 | archive-date = October 10, 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20191010161900/https://www.aps.org/publications/capitolhillquarterly/201004/fermiaward.cfm | url-status = dead }}</ref>
* [[National Medal of Science]] (2013), presented by U.S. President [[Barack Obama]]<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/obama-honors-recipients-of-science-innovation-and-technology-medals/ | title=Obama honors recipients of science, innovation and technology medals| date=February 2013| publisher =CBS| access-date = March 9, 2013}}</ref>
* [[Charles Stark Draper Prize|Draper Prize]] in engineering (2014).<ref>{{cite web | url = https://nae.edu/105792/2014-Charles-Stark-Draper-Prize-for-Engineering-Recipients|title=2014 Charles Stark Draper Prize for Engineering Recipients | publisher = National Academy of Engineering| access-date = October 10, 2019}}</ref>
* [[Welch Award in Chemistry]] (2017)<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.welch1.org/awards/welch-award-in-chemistry/past-recipients |work=Welch Award in Chemistry |title=Past Award Recipients |access-date=June 22, 2020 }}</ref>
* C.K. Prahalad Award (2017)<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.corporateecoforum.com/c-k-prahalad-award/ |title=Prahalad Award 2017 |work=CEF |access-date=June 22, 2020 }}</ref>
* [[Copley Medal]] of the Royal Society (2019)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2019/05/john-goodenough-wins-2019-copley-medal/|title=Inventor of the lithium-ion battery, Professor John Goodenough, awarded Royal Society's prestigious Copley Medal &#124; Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org}}</ref>
* [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] (2019), alongside [[M. Stanley Whittingham]] and [[Akira Yoshino]]<ref name="NYT-20191009">{{cite news |last=Specia |first=Megan |title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry Honors Work on Lithium-Ion Batteries – John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino were recognized for research that "laid the foundation of a wireless, fossil-fuel-free society." |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/09/science/nobel-prize-chemistry.html |date=October 9, 2019 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=October 9, 2019 }}</ref>

Goodenough was 97 when he received the Nobel Prize. He remains the oldest person ever to have been awarded the prize.
